# Baldwin

*Lamplighter*

## Personality

Quiet, unhurried and fond of the dark hours. He knows every lamp in the city by its flicker.

## Lore

Baldwin is sixty-eight, the lamplighter of the plaza, and he is the last person in Selsior to go to bed and very nearly the first to see the stars come out. Every evening at dusk he crosses the plaza with his ladder over one shoulder, his oil can in one hand and his long brass taper in the other, and one by one the lamps around the Great Bell come alight behind him. He does not hurry. He has never hurried in his life, and the lamps, he says, have never minded waiting.

### Fifty years of dusk

He took up the work at eighteen, fifty years ago, as the helper of an old lamplighter called Odo, who carried the ladder for a season before he let Baldwin touch a wick. Odo taught him that every lamp has its own temper: this one smokes if you trim it short, that one gutters in an east wind, the one by the palace steps burns blue for no reason anyone has ever found. Odo has been dead for many years. Baldwin still trims the palace-steps lamp the way Odo showed him and still does not know why it burns blue.

He knows every lamp in the city by its flicker. Not only the plaza's: when the plaza is lit he takes the long way home, through the old quarters, and lights more as he goes, down the winding streets and under the skywalks, so that by the time he reaches his own narrow house near the gate end of the city he has left a thread of light behind him through half of Selsior. The children of the old quarters know that when Baldwin's lamps are lit, Winifred will be out on her doorstep with a story, and they run ahead of him to get there first.

### The people of the dark hours

He is quiet, unhurried and fond of the dark hours, and he has the dark hours' friends. Ida of the night watch passes him most nights in the old quarters with her lantern and her stick, and the two of them exchange a nod and, on a long night, a sentence. Gilbert the candlemaker supplies his oil and wicks and hums while he measures them out; lately Gilbert's bees have been short-tempered, and Baldwin, who has noticed that the night moths behave oddly too, has said so, once, and left it at that.

His brother Hugh is the Warden of the Great Bell, and so the two of them share the plaza: Hugh by day, polishing the bell's dais every morning, and Baldwin by dusk, lighting the lamps around it while Mirabel dances and Fulke plays. Baldwin has listened to his brother and the dancer argue about whether the Bell hums for years. He has never taken a side. He has noticed, on still evenings, that Hugh goes very quiet when the light fails, and he has never asked him why. They are brothers; some things you leave lit and walk past.

Baldwin never married. He says he has a few hundred lamps to look after and that is family enough.

### The lamps by the gate

Lately Baldwin has started leaving extra lamps burning near the city gate. Nobody asked him to. He buys the oil from Gilbert out of his own pocket, sets the lamps on the last stretch of the road inside the gate and in the gatehouse's shadow, and lights them on his way home. He says it is for travellers who come in late, and it is. He does not say the rest of it, which is that he has spent fifty years watching the dark, and he has started to think the dark beyond the gate is not as empty as it used to be. Just in case, he says, and lights another.

### What he wants and fears

Baldwin wants to find someone to carry the ladder, as he once carried Odo's. What he fears is a night when he reaches the gate and the lamps he left burning have been put out.

A quest might begin with one of the plaza lamps refusing to stay lit, the first in fifty years, or with Baldwin asking a traveller to walk the gate road with him after dark, just to see what is out there just past the light.
